study_identification.title: Individualized resting-state functional connectivity abnormalities unveil two major depressive disorder subtypes with contrasting abnormal patterns of abnormality

study_characteristics.study_objective: This study aimed to identify MDD subtypes based on subject-level functional connectivity abnormalities using a tolerance interval-based approach, leveraging a large multi-site dataset of resting-state MRI to detect distinct patterns of neurobiological disturbances.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Standard fMRI preprocessing protocols; Craddock 200 brain atlas; global signal regression was not applied; pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients transformed to Fisher Z scores

quality_checking_detail.answer: Mean framewise displacement (mean FD) used as motion covariate; mean FD for HC: 0.13±0.01; controlled for head motion (mean FD) in statistical analyses

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: ComBat method was applied to harmonize functional connections across 25 research sites to remove site-related variance while preserving biological variability

modeling_method.answer: Tolerance interval-based approach (nonparametric two-sided tolerance intervals)

response_variable.answer: Functional connectivity (pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients transformed to Fisher Z scores; 200 × 200 functional connectivity matrix based on Craddock 200 brain atlas)

predictor_variables.answer: Tolerance interval method (90% tolerance proportion with 10% confidence level); HC sample used to establish normative ranges

predictor_effects.answer: Not applicable (tolerance interval method does not use predictor variables in traditional sense; normative ranges estimated from HC distribution)

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addressed nuisance structure by using ComBat harmonization to remove site-related variance (mean shifts and variance differences) across 25 research sites. This method has been shown to effectively remove site effects while preserving biological variability. Additionally, head motion (mean FD) was controlled for in statistical analyses.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Given the multi-site nature of the data collection, differences in scans and acquisition protocols could introduce non-biological variability. To address this, we applied the Combat method to harmonize the functional connections across these sites. Combat has been shown to effectively remove site-related variance while preserving biological variability in neuroimaging studies

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study validated the normative model using subsampling validation with 100 iterations of 90% randomly selected MDD patients. This is a same-domain non-independent validation approach as it uses overlapping subsets of the training data. Cluster stability was assessed and found to be significantly higher than chance (stability index 0.39, permutation p < 0.01).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Cluster stability was evaluated using 100 randomly selected subsample (90% of patients) and leave-one-site out validation. Co-occurrence rates between patient pairs across iterations were summarized into a single stability index... The K-means algorithm classified the patients into two subtypes (subtype 1, N = 394; subtype 2, N = 882). Cluster stability was assessed through 100 subsampling iterations, yielding a stability index of 0.39, significantly higher than chance (permutation p < 0.01).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text page 3, lines 86-87; Results page 4, lines 115-117

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study performed leave-one-site-out validation, which can be considered a form of same-domain independent validation as each site is held out and used as a test set. The stability index was 0.44 (permutation p < 0.01), showing robust performance. However, this is still within the same REST-meta-MDD consortium dataset, so it's not fully independent external validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Cluster stability was evaluated using 100 randomly selected subsample (90% of patients) and leave-one-site out validation... Leave-one-site-out validation yielded a stability index of 0.44 (permutation p < 0.01).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main text page 3, lines 86-87; Results page 4, line 117

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study did not validate the normative model (tolerance interval approach) on a completely different dataset or domain outside the REST-meta-MDD consortium. While they tested disease specificity using schizophrenia data from COBRE, this was to demonstrate that extreme functional connectivity patterns are MDD-specific, not to validate the normative modeling approach itself on a different domain.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Finally, to examined whether extreme functional connectivity profile we reported is specific to MDD, we applied the same analysis pipeline to a dataset of schizophrenia patients from Centre for Biomedical Research Excellence (COBRE)... Schizophrenia patients exhibited distinct extreme functional connection profiles, highlighting the specificity of our findings to MDD

deviation_metric.answer: Extreme functional connections defined as connections falling outside nonparametric two-sided tolerance intervals (90% tolerance proportion with 10% confidence level) estimated from HC; consistency rate >95% across 100 subsamples; enrichment analysis based on hypergeometric cumulative distribution function

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Functional enrichment analysis associating extreme connections with cognitive processes/functional terms from Neurosynth (217 terms); permutation testing (10,000 iterations) for significance. Linear regression models exploring relationships between extreme functional connections and clinical characteristics (symptom severity, illness duration, age of onset) with Bonferroni correction. K-means clustering algorithm to identify subtypes based on extreme functional connections. Two-sample t-tests to assess functional connectivity abnormalities for each subtype relative to HCs, controlling for sex, age, study site, and head motion (mean FD), with Bonferroni correction. Linear support vector machines (SVMs) in 100×10-fold cross-validation framework to examine case-control discriminability, with performance compared using two-sample t-tests with Bonferroni correction. Subtype characterization using t-tests or chi-square tests for demographic and clinical variables.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Two robust MDD subtypes were identified with contrasting patterns of functional connectivity: subtype 1 (N=394) showed overall increased connectivity, while subtype 2 (N=882) showed overall decreased connectivity, significantly enhancing case-control discriminability.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study identified 556 extreme functional connections (consistency rate >95%) predominantly between the visual network and frontoparietal network, default mode network and ventral attention network, with key nodes in anterior cingulate cortex, bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, and supramarginal gyrus. These connections were significantly enriched in reward, motivation, and pain processes (all permutation p<0.05) and associated with age of onset (adjusted R²=0.39, F=2.13, Bonferroni corrected p<0.01). Two subtypes with contrasting patterns were identified: Subtype 1 exhibited overall increased functional connectivity in 19,579 of 19,900 connections, with abnormalities most pronounced within visual network and between visual network and DMN, frontoparietal and ventral attention networks. Subtype 2 exhibited overall decreased functional connectivity in 15,405 of 19,900 connections with similar network-level patterns. When all patients were analyzed together, no significant differences in functional connectivity were found (Bonferroni corrected p<0.05). The subtypes did not differ significantly in demographic or clinical characteristics, though illness duration difference approached significance (subtype 1 vs. 2: 41.61±68.65m vs. 34.22±55.23m, uncorrected p=0.07). Classification accuracy was 71.66% for subtype 1 vs. HC, 63.26% for subtype 2 vs. HC, and 55.10% for all patients vs. HC, with subtype-specific models significantly outperforming the overall model (both Bonferroni corrected p<0.01). Between-subtype classification accuracy was 92.92%. Results were reproducible with 90% consistency threshold (ARI=0.97) and in untreated patients, with disease-specificity confirmed against schizophrenia data from COBRE.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Only cross-sectional data were analyzed, raising questions about temporal stability of subtypes. Limited clinical data prevented examination of other potential between-subtype differences such as reward processing. Confounding factors including smoking and drinking were not available. Only patients without comorbid mental disorders were included, so impact of comorbidities remains unexplored. Longitudinal studies needed to confirm robustness and explore treatment responses and disease progression.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This is the first study to identify MDD subtypes using subject-level functional connectivity abnormalities based on a large, multi-site neuroimaging dataset. The tolerance interval method offers advantages over traditional group-level approaches by not requiring predefined regions of interest, complex models, or preset parameters. The identified subtypes may reflect fundamental brain differences in MDD not captured by conventional clinical criteria and have yet-to-be-discovered clinical implications. The subtypes provide new perspectives on neurophysiological heterogeneity of MDD and may explain previous conflicting findings regarding DMN alterations and hypo- versus hyperconnectivity in MDD. Unlike symptom-based subtypes which often show overlapping abnormalities, these neuroimaging-based subtypes demonstrate clear brain connectivity differences despite similar clinical profiles.

general_notes.general_notes: This study represents a novel application of tolerance interval-based normative modeling to identify individual-level functional connectivity abnormalities in MDD using a large multi-site dataset (25 sites, 1276 MDD patients, 1104 HC). The REST-meta-MDD consortium data is publicly available at https://www.scidb.cn/en/detail?dataSetId=cbeb3c7124bf47a6af7b3236a3aaf3a8. The MDD cohort included diverse clinical presentations: 538 first-episode individuals, 282 recurrent cases, 447 medication-naive patients, and 408 treated patients. MDD diagnoses were made by experienced psychiatrists according to DSM-IV criteria, with symptom severity assessed using HAMD (mean 20.50±7.66). The study utilized preprocessed mean time courses for 200 brain regions from Craddock atlas, with functional networks estimated by pairwise Pearson correlations transformed to Fisher Z scores. The study demonstrated robustness through multiple validation approaches: subsampling (stability index 0.39, p<0.01), leave-one-site-out (stability index 0.44, p<0.01), varying consistency thresholds (90% vs 95%), and validation in untreated patients. Disease specificity was confirmed by comparing to schizophrenia patients from COBRE dataset (72 patients, 74 HC), which showed distinct spatial patterns of extreme functional connections. The identified subtypes challenge prevailing theories of hypoconnectivity in MDD and may explain discrepancies in previous studies. The extreme functional connections were consistently selected across 100 subsamples with 90% of patients in each iteration using enrichment analysis based on hypergeometric cumulative distribution function.
